From Open Labs to Closed Empires?

How the Large Language Model Frontier Changed (2023–2026): An Exploratory Visual Analytics Investigation
Final Project Report — Group 3
Structure: Part I — Overall Work (excluding Cover and References)  |  Part II — Individual Contributions (1 page per member)
Submission Package: Combined Final Report PDF, Local Runnable Web Platform (work_package/), and AI Usage Disclosure Report
Date: 28 November 2026  ·  Data Cut-off: Frozen public datasets through September 2026
Abstract

Between May 2023 and September 2026, the top tier of the LM Arena text leaderboard shifted from open-weight academic and community models to a Top 10 occupied entirely by proprietary models from three organizations. Popular commentary often characterizes this shift as a monotonic collapse of open-weight artificial intelligence into closed corporate monopolies. To test that narrative rigorously, we developed an interactive, five-chapter visual analytics platform integrating eight frozen public data families—covering leaderboard trajectories, corporate market capitalization, audited SEC 10-K revenues, private-lab revenue run rates, mapped corporate AI publications, Epoch AI training-cost and compute estimates, Hugging Face model repository supply, national AI talent netflow, and U.S. Census business AI adoption.

Through iterative visual exploration, hypothesis testing, and entity-level cross-filtering, we show that a binary “open-to-closed extinction” thesis is empirically untenable. Instead, our evidence supports a bifurcated structure—“Closed Frontier, Open Commons”: while proprietary models captured 100% of the September 2026 Arena Top 10 alongside estimated frontier training costs of $218M–$388M+ and an academic notable-model share contraction from 15.1% to 1.1%, open-weight models retained 18% of the Top 50 (9/50), briefly reclaimed rank #1 via DeepSeek R1 in early 2025, and nearly tripled quarterly Hugging Face supply to 332,098 new repositories in 2025Q4. Across all views, we enforce strict epistemic discipline by separating non-equivalent denominators, encoding missingness explicitly, and avoiding causal over-claiming.

Keywords: Visual Analytics, Large Language Models, Open-Weight vs. Proprietary Frontier, Exploratory Data Analysis, Coordinated Multiple Views, Epistemic Uncertainty

Part I · Overall Work

1. Introduction, Project Objectives, and Key Contributions

The rapid commercialization of large language models (LLMs) between 2023 and 2026 reshaped both benchmark leadership and the institutional geography of frontier AI development. In May 2023, the earliest public LM Arena leaderboard snapshot contained ten open-weight community and university models led by LMSYS's vicuna-13b and UC Berkeley's koala-13b [1, 8]. By September 2026, all ten top-ranked text models belonged to proprietary API systems operated by just three corporations: Anthropic (7 models), Google (2 models), and Meta (1 model) [1]. Yet treating this endpoint contrast as proof that open-weight AI has vanished risks conflating apex leaderboard concentration with ecosystem-wide disappearance.

This project constructs a locally runnable, five-chapter exploratory visual analytics report—From Open Labs to Closed Empires?—designed to investigate how and why the LLM frontier changed across 2023–2026. Specifically, our work pursues three formal objectives:

  1. Measure the leaderboard transition with granularity: Track how Arena rank composition, weight-access tiers (permissive open, restricted open, proprietary), and the signed open-versus-closed frontier rank gap evolved across 41 monthly snapshots and 29 task categories rather than relying on binary start-versus-end bar charts.
  2. Contextualize benchmark leadership against multi-source structural evidence: Examine organizational financial expansion, corporate AI publication trends, estimated pre-training costs and compute ceilings, institutional funding benchmarks, recorded evaluation attention, open-platform repository supply, national AI talent netflow, and U.S. employer-business AI adoption side by side.
  3. Enforce visual-analytics epistemic rigor: Prevent misleading composite scores, dual-axis denominator mixing, and causal over-claiming by preserving source-specific units, encoding incomplete or missing intervals visibly, and embedding live robustness checks directly inside each chapter's interactive dashboard.

1.1 Summary of Principal Contributions

  • Empirical Reframing (“Closed Frontier, Open Commons”): Iterative visual analysis overturned our initial hypothesis of a monotonic open-weight collapse. While the September 2026 Top 10 was 100% proprietary, open-weight models retained 18% of the Top 50 (9/50; 16% strictly Apache/MIT), briefly reclaimed rank #1 via DeepSeek R1 in Jan–Feb 2025, and expanded quarterly Hugging Face repository supply nearly threefold from 118,252 (2024Q1) to 332,098 (2025Q4) [1, 2, 6].
  • Unified State-Preserving Visual Analytics Platform: We integrated five independently engineered chapter dashboards (D3/Canvas + SVG in Ch1; Apache ECharts in Ch2–Ch5) inside a shared Flask/Waitress web shell with persistent iframes, unified color and typography tokens, synchronized cross-filtering, brush-and-link controls, and automated QA across 20 API hashes, 77 chart instances, and 30 responsive screenshots.
  • Epistemic Transparency Encoded in Every View: Missing snapshot months appear hatched rather than interpolated; incomplete late-period series (2025 ETO publications, 2026 Arena vote extensions) render dashed; survey estimates display 90% confidence intervals (±1.645 SE); and private AI labs remain explicitly blank in listed-company market views rather than receiving fabricated valuations.

Because combining eight heterogeneous datasets invites severe visual-analytics pitfalls—most notably hidden denominator shifts and spurious cross-series subtraction—every chart across Chapters 1–5 obeys four shared analytical rules:

Rule 1 · Overall-Only Core Rankings. Primary leaderboard metrics in Ch1, Ch4, and Ch5 use Arena's overall category exclusively to prevent double-counting across overlapping subcategories, which remain accessible via Ch1's category selector.
Rule 2 · Explicit Missingness Encoding. Underfilled pre-Feb 2024 pools are never rescaled to 100% of a Top 50; missing snapshot months render hatched; incomplete 2025 publications render dashed; unknown licenses remain a distinct category.
Rule 3 · Strict Unit Separation. Market capitalization, audited 10-K revenue, annualized run rates, evaluation vote share, and HF repository counts occupy separate panels and axes—never subtracted or collapsed into one composite score.
Rule 4 · Triangulation Over Causal Claims. Aligned timing across financial, compute, and adoption tracks illuminates structural barriers without asserting unobserved user migration or formal causal identification.

3. Visual Storyline, Interactive Analysis, and Derivation of Findings

Our visual narrative unfolds as a five-stage empirical inquiry rather than a static showcase of disconnected charts. We begin by verifying the surface phenomenon—the apparent takeover of the LM Arena frontier by proprietary labs (Section 3.1)—and immediately discover that the shift is neither monotonic nor total. This observation motivates three targeted structural comparisons: how corporate commercial scale diverged from corporate academic publishing (Section 3.2); whether escalating training costs and compute thresholds erected a capital barrier that priced academia out of frontier pre-training (Section 3.3); and whether broader ecosystem attention, open-model supply, talent flows, and business adoption moved in lockstep or in parallel (Section 3.4). Finally, Section 3.5 brings all threads together in a two-view synthesis dashboard that subjects our overarching thesis—Closed Frontier, Open Commons—to organization-by-organization interactive verification.

3.1 Chapter 1 — The Flip: Measuring the Leaderboard Shift

Storyline Role and Visual Encoding. Any explanation of why the LLM frontier centralized must first establish what actually changed—and avoid distorting the baseline. Early project drafts compared only the May 2023 and September 2026 Top 10 snapshots, which produced an overly dramatic narrative of open-weight extinction because the May 2023 pool contained just 10 models and lacked comprehensive closed-model coverage. To correct this bias, Chapter 1 pairs two complementary visual levels. First, Figure 2 summarizes the macro trajectory across two quantitative panels: Panel A plots the monthly percentage of open-weight models inside the full-pool Arena overall Top 50 strictly from February 2024 onward (when the leaderboard pool first reached ≥50 models), while Panel B plots the signed frontier rank gap—defined as the rank of the highest-placed open-weight model minus the rank of the highest-placed closed-weight model—anchored around a zero parity line from December 2023 through September 2026 [1].

Second, to let analysts inspect individual releases, tied ranks, and license nuances behind these aggregates, Figure 3 presents the delivered Chapter 1 interactive dashboard (/explore/ch1/), engineered with D3 scales on HTML5 Canvas paired with an accessible SVG monthly ruler. Each horizontal column represents one monthly snapshot (41 months total) and each discrete tile represents one ranked model (green for open-weight, terracotta for closed-weight, gray border for rank ties). Crucially, underfilled pre-2024 rows remain visually empty rather than stretched, missing snapshot months display hatched gray bands, and a dashed vertical marker at 2023.12 delimits incomplete early closed-weight recording.

How We Derived the Conclusions. Reading Figures 2 and 3 together led directly to a substantial revision of our initial Hypothesis H1. First, restricting Panel 2A to full ≥50-model pools immediately eliminated the spurious “100% baseline” illusion and showed that the open-weight Top-50 share fell from 80% (40/50 in Feb 2024) to 18% (9/50 in Sep 2026) through several mid-2025 rebounds rather than a smooth monotonic decline. Second, auditing the final September 2026 snapshot (401 models) revealed that while the Top 10 became 100% closed-weight across just three organizations—Anthropic (7 models, led by claude-fable-5.1-max), Google (2 models), and Meta (1 model, muse-spark-1.2)—nine open-weight models remained competitive inside the Top 50 at ranks 17, 22, 23, 28, 31, 32, 36, 42, and 50 (16% under strict Apache/MIT licenses). Third, computing the signed frontier gap (Figure 2B) uncovered a sharp counter-example: after widening from +2 ranks (Dec 2023) to +10 (Oct 2024), the gap inverted to −1 in January–February 2025 when open-weight DeepSeek R1 briefly held #1 overall before proprietary releases reopened a +16 rank lead by September 2026. Thus, our first conclusion is carefully bounded: proprietary concentration is complete at the very top (Top 10), but open-weight models remain active across the broader frontier (Top 50) and have periodically contested #1.

3.2 Chapter 2 — Divergence: Commercial Scale vs. Corporate Academic Output

Storyline Transition and Visual Encoding. Observing that three capital-intensive corporations monopolized the September 2026 Top 10 naturally raises the next question in our storyline: how did the economic scale and open-research publishing behavior of leading AI organizations evolve during this same window? An early proposal plan sought to rank Big-7 incumbents and smaller labs along a single unified “organizational development index.” Schema verification immediately showed why that design was invalid: private frontier labs (OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Mistral AI) have no public stock market capitalization, and reported annualized revenue run rates are not comparable to audited GAAP 10-K revenue. Chapter 2 therefore separates these incompatible measures into four coordinated ECharts views inside /explore/ch2/ (Figure 4): (2.1) listed-company monthly market capitalization, audited SEC 10-K annual revenue, and within-cohort share stacks for five public AI leaders (NVIDIA, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta); (2.2) private AI-lab annualized revenue run rates with an explicit linear/log scale toggle; (2.3) max-year revenue scale context; and (2.4) ETO mapped yearly corporate AI publications (2023–2025), plotting complete 2023–2024 trajectories as solid lines and flagging incomplete 2025 records (Complete=False) as dashed segments [2, 5, 7].

How We Derived the Conclusions. Placing commercial expansion directly beside mapped corporate publishing revealed a striking structural divergence. On the commercial side, inspecting reconstructed monthly market caps (Jan 2023–Sep 2026) showed massive, broad-based valuation gains across all five listed infrastructure and frontier leaders: NVIDIA expanded 11.0× ($479B → $5.27T), Meta 4.3× ($387B → $1.65T), Alphabet 3.2× ($1.28T → $4.14T), Amazon 2.6× ($1.05T → $2.77T), and Microsoft 2.1× ($1.79T → $3.68T), backed by audited SEC 10-K revenue expansion (e.g., NVIDIA rising 8.0× from $27.0B in FY23 to $215.9B in FY26; Amazon growing from $574.8B to $716.9B) [5]. Simultaneously, toggling Panel 2.2 confirmed that leading private labs experienced explosive top-line scaling on their own reported run-rate track—OpenAI climbing from $0.2B (Mar 2023) to $25.0B (Feb 2026) and Anthropic from $0.1B (Oct 2023) to $19.0B (Mar 2026)—while smaller challengers such as xAI ($0.43B), Mistral AI ($0.40B), and Z.ai ($0.05B) remained one to two orders of magnitude smaller [2].

Conversely, auditing Panel 2.4 strictly within complete ETO reporting years (2023 → 2024, thereby avoiding 2025 truncation artifacts) uncovered steep, synchronized contractions in corporate AI research publications: Alphabet/Google declined 33.9% (951 → 629), Alibaba/Qwen fell 37.7% (727 → 453), Meta dropped 25.7% (439 → 326), and OpenAI fell 40.9% (22 → 13), with dashed 2025 observations trending lower still [7]. Taken together, these parallel trajectories yield our second finding: as frontier LLM development shifted from exploratory research to multi-billion-dollar commercialization, major corporate labs expanded rapidly in financial scale while simultaneously reducing open academic publication output.

3.3 Chapter 3 — The Cost Cliff: Training Economics and Academic Exit

Storyline Transition and Visual Encoding. Chapter 2 establishes commercial concentration and declining corporate publishing, but does not yet explain why universities and small independent laboratories—which dominated the May 2023 Arena Top 10—largely disappeared from the frontier. Chapter 3 tests the central structural mechanism of our storyline: did escalating pre-training compute and capital costs cross a threshold that priced academia and smaller labs out of frontier pre-training?

Because frontier training costs and institutional funding spans cover three to four orders of magnitude, linear scales crush academic observations onto the horizontal axis. Figure 5 displays the five-panel Chapter 3 dashboard (/explore/ch3/), built around logarithmic encoding and consistent sector colors (terracotta for Industry, slate blue for Academia): (3.1) a log-scale scatter plot of estimated training cost in 2023 USD across n = 288 notable models ≥$0.8M released in 2023–2026 (254 Industry, 34 Academia), filling missing direct cost estimates via a transparent FLOP proxy ($4×10−18/FLOP), distinguishing open-weight models (diamonds) from closed-weight models (circles), and fitting an empirical exponential trendline (~1.83×/yr across this subset); (3.2) a log-scale lollipop chart benchmarking total institutional funding or illustrative university HPC budgets against a single $366M GPT-4.5 training run (vertical dashed 1.0× reference line); and three aligned bottom context panels from the 2026 Stanford AI Index: (3.3a) notable AI model origin shares by sector, (3.3b) industry-versus-academia training compute ceilings in FLOPs, and (3.3c) frontier lab annual spending ($B) [2, 3, 10].

How We Derived the Conclusions. Synthesizing all five panels builds an internally consistent economic barrier argument while preserving strict methodological caveats. First, inspecting the upper envelope of Panel 3.1 showed estimated single-run pre-training costs rising roughly ~2.4×/yr among frontier releases (~1.83×/yr across all 288 models ≥$0.8M), reaching $218M (Grok 3), $264M (GPT-5), $366M (GPT-4.5), and $388M (Grok 4) [3]. Second, mapping institutional capital onto the 1.0× GPT-4.5 benchmark in Panel 3.2 demonstrated an order-of-magnitude mismatch: illustrative academic budgets sit at 0.005× ($2M lab) to 0.041× ($15M top university HPC), and even venture-backed startups such as AI21 Labs (0.82×) and Runway (0.86×) fall below a single $366M frontier run, whereas frontier incumbents scaled total annual expenditures dramatically—Anthropic from $2.5B to $7.0B and OpenAI from $4.0B to $16.0B between 2024 and 2025 (Panel 3.3c) [2, 10]. Third, cross-reading Panels 3.3a and 3.3b linked this capital gap directly to institutional output: academic pre-training runs clustered beneath an observable ~1024 FLOP ceiling while industry pushed to 1025–1026+ FLOPs, coinciding with a collapse in academia's standalone share of notable AI models from 15.1% (2023) to 3.1% (2024) and 1.1% (2025) as industry's share expanded from 58.0% to 91.6% [2]. Following our epistemic rules, we frame this as strong barrier evidence consistent with academic exit from frontier pre-training—explicitly noting that modeled costs rely in part on FLOP proxies and that total institutional funding is an order-of-magnitude benchmark rather than an audited single-run budget.

3.4 Chapter 4 — Parallel Trends: Ecosystem Attention, Open Supply, Talent, and Adoption

Storyline Transition and Visual Encoding. Chapters 1–3 show that frontier pre-training centralized behind steep capital barriers. Our initial proposal hypothesized a corresponding ecosystem “scissors gap” (H4/H4b): as closed models dominated the leaderboard, developer and user activity would migrate away from open models while open-source supply stagnated. Testing that hypothesis required examining four distinct real-world populations—Arena evaluators, Hugging Face model uploaders, international AI researchers, and U.S. employer businesses—without falsely merging their incompatible denominators.

Figure 6 shows the delivered Chapter 4 dashboard (/explore/ch4/) in its default 2024–2025 comparison window, which coordinates global temporal controls (preset windows 2024–25, Battle window, All dates, drag-to-brush timeline zoom, and click-to-pin cross-panel date alignment) with semantically scoped panel controls (model selectors affect only Panel 4.2 Exposure; country selectors affect only Panel 4.3 Talent; toggles expose Fixed 61, Full weeks, 90% interval, and Events). To display the complete longitudinal context across every source's full window without visual clutter, Figure 7 extracts the four full-window trajectories directly from the SHA256-verified Chapter 4 data manifest [1, 2, 4, 6].

Together, these four tracks establish our fourth finding: proprietary evaluation concentration and open-ecosystem creation are expanding in parallel alongside broader enterprise AI adoption, refuting a zero-sum “closed replaces open” model.

3.5 Chapter 5 — Synthesis: Stress-Testing “Closed Frontier, Open Commons”

Storyline Culmination and Visual Encoding. Chapters 1 through 4 examine macro trajectories across separate domains, leaving a critical question unresolved: when we follow individual organizations across leaderboard rank, training cost, recorded evaluation attention, and public market context simultaneously, where do the four evidentiary tracks align—and where does data coverage legitimately end? During iterative design, we deliberately retired our early proposal idea of a single wide table and causal arrow diagram because private labs lack stock tickers, cost records are sparse, and collapsing heterogeneous units into one composite index obscures exceptions. Instead, Chapter 5 delivers a streamlined, two-view interactive synthesis dashboard (/dashboard/ch5/) covering 22 organizations (7 frontier Big-7 labs and 15 smaller/community labs).

View 1 — Macro Anchor (The shift, Figure 8). Panel 5.2 vertically links quarterly proprietary Arena vote share (including the dashed Fixed-61 check and dashed 2026 extension) with quarterly new Hugging Face repositories—encapsulating the dual “Closed Frontier, Open Commons” pattern in a single view.

Synthesis Verdict — How Five Chapters Converge on “Closed Frontier, Open Commons”: Comparing View 1's macro totals against View 2's live entity cross-checks—contrasting listed hyperscalers (Google, Meta, which later re-entered the Sep 2026 Top 10 via proprietary muse-spark-1.2) against private proprietary leaders (Anthropic at #1 and 16.9% vote share) and cost-efficient open challengers (DeepSeek at #1 in early 2025 on $6.8M open runs)—explains why neither “open-source triumph” nor “closed monopoly extinction” fits the evidence. Frontier leadership at the very apex (Top 10) concentrated among capital-rich proprietary labs amid escalating $100M–$388M+ training runs and declining corporate academic publishing, yet an energetic open-weight commons continues to supply 18% of the Top 50, periodically challenge #1 at dramatically lower reported compute cost, and expand quarterly Hugging Face releases toward 332k/quarter.

4. Effectiveness: Hypothesis Verification and Knowledge Discovery

A core criterion of visual analytics effectiveness is whether interactive visual exploration actively tests, refines, or falsifies initial hypotheses rather than merely illustrating predetermined conclusions. Table 2 traces how our five proposal-stage hypotheses evolved directly through exploratory visual analysis across Chapters 1–5.

Table 2. Traceability from initial proposal hypotheses to evidence-revised conclusions via exploratory visual analysis.
Chapter / Hyp. Initial Proposal Hypothesis Interactive Visual Analysis Outcome Revised Claim & Knowledge Discovery
Ch1 · H1 / H1′
Leaderboard Flip		 Open-weight share collapsed monotonically from ~100% to <20% around a single flip point. Monthly rank blocks, 3-tier composition, Apache/MIT toggle, and signed frontier gap (Dec 2023–Sep 2026). Revised Top 10 is 100% closed (3 orgs), but Top 50 stayed 18% (9/50), early pools had <50 models, and DeepSeek R1 briefly took #1 (−1 gap) in Jan–Feb 2025.
Ch2 · H2
Scale Divergence		 Big-7 vs. small labs can be compared on one unified market-scale & output trajectory. Separated listed market cap & 10-K revenue, private-lab run rates, and ETO publications with completeness flags. Refined Both public giants and top private labs grew rapidly on distinct financial scales, while complete-year corporate AI publications fell −26% to −38% (2023→2024).
Ch3 · H3 / H3b
Cost Cliff		 Exponential training costs crossed a threshold that priced academia out of frontier pre-training. Log cost scatter with Open/Closed filter, $366M funding multiples, 1024 FLOP ceiling, and AI Index origin shares. Consistent Frontier costs reach $218M–$388M+, academic funding sits at 0.005×–0.041×, and academic notable-model share fell 15.1%→1.1% (2023–25); framed as barrier evidence.
Ch4 · H4 / H4b
Ecosystem Shift		 User attention migrated to closed models while open supply stalled (“scissors gap”). 4-panel linked date brush, Fixed-61 check, 140k weekly exposure, U.S. talent netflow, and BTOS Q7 with 90% CI. Reframed Proprietary evaluation share (+5.89 pp; Fixed-61 +13.49 pp) and HF supply (118k→332k/qtr) grew together; BTOS adoption rose 3.7%→10.0% without proving vendor choice.
Ch5 · H5
Synthesis		 A single institution-month wide table & causal chain diagram can summarize all mechanisms. 2-page linked entity explorer across 22 orgs comparing rank, cost, votes, and listed market index side by side. Reframed Replaces causal arrows with inspectable multi-track alignment (“Closed Frontier, Open Commons”) where missing coverage remains explicitly blank.

Operationally, the platform implements Shneiderman's Visual Information-Seeking Mantra—overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand [12]—by opening every chapter with concise Storyboard overview charts before expanding into state-preserving interactive dashboards equipped with live robustness toggles: Top 10 vs. Top 50 and Apache/MIT detail (Ch1), greyed-out cohort denominators (Ch2), Open vs. Closed cost filtering (Ch3), Fixed-61 and Full-weeks toggles (Ch4), and Log vs. Linear rank scaling (Ch5).

5. System Architecture, Design Trade-Offs, and Unimplemented Plans

5.1 Implemented Platform Architecture and Quality Verification

The delivered artifact (work_package/) is a self-contained web application served locally by Python Flask + Waitress (app.py mounting Ch2 and Ch3 via Werkzeug DispatcherMiddleware alongside static and JSON API routes for Storyboard, Ch1, Ch4, and Ch5). All visualization libraries (Apache ECharts, D3.js), local InterVariable webfonts, and frozen extracts ship offline with zero external CDN calls. Shared design tokens (chart-theme.css, chart-theme.js, embed.css) unify visual encodings across modules, while a custom embed-bridge.js protocol keeps chapter iframes alive in place across collapse, expansion, and fullscreen transitions so users never lose zoom, brush, or filter state. Prior to packaging, automated and visual QA (work_package/VERIFICATION.md) confirmed that all 20 API endpoints and 121 bundled data/public files matched baseline SHA256 hashes, 77 rendered chart instances preserved exact values and axes, MutationObserver tests recorded zero iframe reloads across mode switches, and 30 Playwright screenshots verified zero horizontal overflow across five viewports (1920×1080 to 390×844).

5.3 Key Difficulties Encountered and Unimplemented Plans

Four recurring engineering and analytical challenges shaped the project: (1) cross-source entity alignment across 10 raw datasets with inconsistent organization labels (e.g., Alphabet (including Google) in ETO, multi-org strings in Epoch AI, and 61 drifting model-to-organization mappings in LM Arena), solved via explicit crosswalks that leave unmapped entities blank rather than zero-imputed; (2) unifying five independently authored tech stacks (React/Vite in Ch1, Dash/Plotly in Ch2, Flask/Plotly in Ch3, standalone HTML/JS in Ch4, ECharts in Ch5) into one coherent shell via Ruan Lixin's refactor (PR #1) and member PRs (#2–#9); (3) reconciling staggered end dates (Arena Sep 2026; BTOS & Talent Sep 2025; HF Dec 2025; ETO 2025 incomplete; SEC FY26 partial) through preset windows and dashed incomplete segments; and (4) disciplining causal prose during rehearsals so every headline remains strictly bounded by empirical measurement.

6. Limitations and Future Work

6.1 Data and Measurement Limitations

  • Leaderboard and evaluation validity (Ch1, Ch4): LM Arena pools evolve continuously, and platform scoring/sampling policies changed on 2024-01-09, 2025-05-16 (default style control), and 2025-07-23. Rank differences are ordinal rather than cardinal capability margins; “open-weight” does not imply OSI-compliant open training data or unrestricted commercial rights; and 22.4% of adjacent leaderboard vote-count deltas are negative, reflecting platform sampling rather than real-world market share.
  • Economic, cost, and adoption validity (Ch2, Ch3, Ch4): Epoch AI training costs blend direct estimates with FLOP-based proxies ($4×10−18/FLOP) and exclude post-training, data curation, and inference expenses. The $366M GPT-4.5 benchmark is illustrative, and cumulative venture funding is not liquid capital dedicated to one pre-training run. Hugging Face repository additions measure upload volume (including fine-tunes and adapters) rather than frontier capability, while Census BTOS measures broad U.S. business AI usage rather than LLM-specific adoption.

6.2 Visualization and Tooling Limitations

  • Canvas pixel rendering vs. vector accessibility (Ch1): HTML5 Canvas delivers smooth 60 fps D3 morphing across 2,050 rank blocks, but Canvas pixels cannot be natively searched, screen-read, or exported as vector paths; pairing Canvas with an accessible SVG hover ruler and an HTML monthly detail table mitigates this trade-off.
  • Logarithmic scale trade-offs (Ch2, Ch3, Ch5): Log axes make 1,000× cost and funding ranges readable, yet exclude non-positive values and visually compress large absolute dollar gaps at the top end (mitigated via explicit Linear/Log toggles in Ch2 and Ch5).
  • Iframe shell and local server dependency: Keeping five dashboards mounted in persistent iframes preserved member autonomy and interactive state, but requires cross-frame height/scroll synchronization (embed-bridge.js) and a local Python server (bash start.sh) rather than a single serverless HTML file; frozen September 2026 extracts also cap currency.

6.3 Prioritized Future Work

Future iterations should: (1) audit and freeze machine-readable license taxonomies distinguishing open weights, training data, and code model-by-model; (2) incorporate longitudinal enterprise API or cloud telemetry once publicly available to bridge the firm-to-model adoption gap; (3) propagate explicit cost-estimation confidence intervals onto Chapter 3's scatter and funding-multiple views; and (4) compile a static WebAssembly/Pyodide or pre-computed JSON build enabling full serverless hosting on GitHub Pages.
